# Abstract

This gazetteer compiles population estimates for 1.236 cities, industrial towns, railway junctions and ports across the 48 provinces of Late Imperial Russia and Austro-Hungarian Ukraine at five benchmark dates between the Congress of Vienna in 1815AD and the Russian Revolution of 1917AD. Before the emancipation of the serfs in the 1860s, urban growth remained modest outside Saint Petersburg, Moscow, Warsaw, Odessa and Riga. Over the next half-century, railway building, coal and steel works in the Donbas and Congress Poland, the Grozny and Boryslav oil booms and peasant migration along the Trans-Siberian line transformed the urban map. By 1914AD, Saint Petersburg (2,12M) and Moscow (1,76M) led an urban network that included Warsaw (884,5k), Odessa (630k), Kyiv (626,3k), Riga (517,5k) and the textile and mining boomtowns of Lodz (477,9k), Sosnowiec (118,5k) and Yuzovka (54k), before the First World War emptied frontline cities in Poland, Courland and Lithuania and swelled interior towns with more than 6M refugees [@Troinitsky1905Goroda; @TsSK1915; @Rashin1956; @Gatrell1999].

# Methodology

This gazetteer traces the population histories of 1.236 towns, industrial centres, ports and fortresses across the 48 provinces of Late Imperial Russia and Austro-Hungarian Ukraine (excluding Central Asia and the Southern Caucasus) from the Congress of Vienna in 1815AD to the revolutions of 1917AD. Each town is listed under its historical name alongside its local and modern equivalents, geographic coordinates and population estimates for 1815AD, 1858AD, 1897AD, 1914AD and 1917AD.

The town figures draw on the main fiscal and statistical surveys of the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries: the Seventh (1815-1816AD), Eighth (1833-1835AD) and Tenth (1857-1858AD) Imperial Soul Revisions and Ministry of Internal Affairs town tables [@Troinitsky1861; @Kabuzan1971; @Rashin1956], the First All-Russian General Census of 28 January 1897AD across all 89 provincial volumes and its companion register of settlements over 500 inhabitants [@Troinitsky1905; @Troinitsky1905Goroda], the 1 January 1914AD yearbooks of the Central Statistical Committee and the Warsaw Statistical Committee [@TsSK1915; @WarsawStat1914], the ten-year censuses of the Finnish Statistical Office [@FinlandStat1870_1915], the Austrian and Hungarian censuses of 1869-1910AD for Galicia, Bukovina and Subcarpathia [@OsterreichischeStatistik1912; @MagyarStatisztika1912] and the 1916-1917AD All-Russian Urban and Agricultural Censuses paired with Tatiana Committee wartime refugee records [@AgCensus1917; @Gatrell1999]. Industrial, coal-mining, railway and northern ports founded after 1815AD - such as Bodaibo (1864AD), Yuzovka (1869AD), Novonikolaevsk (1893AD), Belotsarsk (1914AD) and Romanov-on-Murman (1916AD) - are marked `-` at dates prior to their establishment.



# Results

## Warsaw, Plock and Lomza Governorates

Table \ref{tab:reg1-sites} gives the populations of the 32 catalogued settlements in the Warsaw, Plock and Lomza governorates, where the regional population grew from 1,02M in 1815AD to 3,54M in 1897AD and 5,05M in 1914AD before falling to 4,42M in 1917AD during the First World War [@WarsawStat1914; @Troinitsky1905Goroda; @Corrsin1989; @Gatrell1999].

## Piotrkow and Kalisz Governorates

Table \ref{tab:reg2-sites} gives the populations of the 19 catalogued settlements in the Piotrkow and Kalisz governorates, where the regional population rose from 720k in 1815AD to 2,25M in 1897AD and 3,32M in 1914AD before dropping to 2,95M in 1917AD [@WarsawStat1914; @Troinitsky1905Goroda; @Corrsin1989; @Gatrell1999].

## Livland Governorate

Table \ref{tab:reg6-sites} gives the populations of the 36 catalogued settlements in Livland Governorate, where the regional population rose from 615k in 1815AD to 1,3M in 1897AD and 1,56M in 1914AD before wartime factory evacuations from Riga reduced it to 1,42M in 1917AD [@Troinitsky1905Goroda; @TsSK1915; @Gortfelder2023BalticFertility; @Gatrell1999].

Table \ref{tab:reg7-sites} gives the populations of the 38 catalogued settlements in Courland Governorate, where the regional population rose from 418k in 1815AD to 674k in 1897AD and 800k in 1914AD before the 1915AD German occupation and refugee flight halved it to 380k in 1917AD [@Troinitsky1905Goroda; @TsSK1915; @Gortfelder2023BalticFertility; @Gatrell1999].

## Southern Finland: Nyland, Abo-Bjorneborg, Tavastehus and Vyborg

Table \ref{tab:reg8-sites} gives the populations of the 45 catalogued settlements in southern Finland (Nyland, Abo-Bjorneborg, Tavastehus and Vyborg provinces), where the regional population grew from 590k in 1815AD to 1,43M in 1897AD, 1,84M in 1914AD and 1,89M in 1917AD [@FinlandStat1870_1915; @Pitkanen1993; @Luostarinen2026FinlandMortality].

## Interior and Northern Finland: Vasa, Kuopio, Sankt-Michel and Uleaborg

Table \ref{tab:reg9-sites} gives the populations of the 46 catalogued settlements in interior and northern Finland (Vasa, Kuopio, Sankt-Michel and Uleaborg provinces), where the regional population rose from 520k in 1815AD to 1,13M in 1897AD, 1,4M in 1914AD and 1,43M in 1917AD [@FinlandStat1870_1915; @Pitkanen1993; @Luostarinen2026FinlandMortality].

## Kovno Governorate

Table \ref{tab:reg10-sites} gives the populations of the 58 catalogued settlements in Kovno Governorate, where the regional population grew from 660k in 1815AD to 1,54M in 1897AD and 1,84M in 1914AD before falling to 1,32M in 1917AD during the First World War [@Troinitsky1905Goroda; @TsSK1915; @Rowland1986; @Gatrell1999].

## Vilna and Grodno Governorates

Table \ref{tab:reg11-sites} gives the populations of the 54 catalogued settlements in the Vilna and Grodno governorates, where the regional population grew from 1,15M in 1815AD to 3,19M in 1897AD and 3,94M in 1914AD before the 1915AD retreat reduced it to 2,88M in 1917AD [@Troinitsky1905Goroda; @TsSK1915; @Rowland1986; @Gatrell1999].

## Minsk Governorate and Pripyat Polesia

Table \ref{tab:reg12-sites} gives the populations of the 18 catalogued settlements in Minsk Governorate, where the regional population grew from 920k in 1815AD to 2,15M in 1897AD and 3,04M in 1914AD before dipping to 2,89M in 1917AD [@Troinitsky1905Goroda; @TsSK1915; @Rowland1986; @Gatrell1999].

## Vitebsk and Mogilev Governorates

Table \ref{tab:reg13-sites} gives the populations of the 38 catalogued settlements in the Vitebsk and Mogilev governorates, where the regional population grew from 1,25M in 1815AD to 3,18M in 1897AD and 4,02M in 1914AD before edging down to 3,86M in 1917AD [@Troinitsky1905Goroda; @TsSK1915; @Rowland1986; @Gatrell1999].

## Austro-Hungarian Eastern Galicia

Table \ref{tab:reg14-sites} gives the populations of the 12 catalogued settlements in Eastern Galicia, where the regional population grew from 2,58M in 1815AD to 4,42M in 1897AD and 5,02M in 1914AD before fighting on the Carpathian and Galician fronts reduced it to 4,45M in 1917AD [@OsterreichischeStatistik1912; @MagyarStatisztika1912; @Himka1988; @Gatrell1999].

## Middle Volga Governorates: Nizhny Novgorod, Kazan, Simbirsk and Penza

Table \ref{tab:reg32-sites} gives the populations of the 50 catalogued settlements in the Nizhny Novgorod, Kazan, Simbirsk and Penza governorates, where the regional population grew from 4,28M in 1815AD to 6,75M in 1897AD, 8,35M in 1914AD and 8,55M in 1917AD [@Troinitsky1905Goroda; @TsSK1915; @Rashin1956; @AgCensus1917].
